BofA’s Hartnett (Flow Show) says “we stay risk-off until rate hikes end/financial conditions ease” through lower oil, yields and the dollar. Where those stand:

▪ Oil: he wants WTI below $70 and says the drop is “underway.” WTI is at $88, down 17% from its Sep 14 high.
▪ Yields: he wants the 10-year Treasury yield below 4.5%, “likely Dec-Jan.” It’s at 5.10%, up 24bp this week.
▪ Dollar: he says it’s “currently moving decisively the other way” and peaks in Feb-Mar. The dollar index is at its highest since April 2025.

He adds that the global tightening cycle (more than 70 rate hikes from June ‘26 to May ‘27) ends at the April FOMC at the earliest.

His bull case for the S&P 500 is above 8,000. It rests on “insatiably buy-the-dip flows” and the equal-weight S&P 500 getting back to its highs, which would show stocks still beat bonds absent a recession or credit event. It also needs the “big stuff” (JNK, SPX, XBD, TSM) to hold at or above their 200-day averages, and the Nov 18 Trump-Xi-Putin meeting at the APEC summit to confirm “peak oil.”

His bear case is below 7,000. It comes from a dollar spike and liquidity shortage, or a “policy mistake as central banks hike into slowdown just as everyone has piled into cyclical ‘quality.’” He says the “quickest way to end the inflationary K-shape consumer & AI capex = higher credit spreads/lower stocks.”

The S&P 500 closed Thursday at 7,592.

Most vulnerable to the downside next eight weeks: high-yield bonds, US and emerging-market stocks, energy, healthcare and mega-cap consumer stocks. 

Most vulnerable to the upside next eight weeks: gold, investment-grade tech bonds, Japan and Europe stocks, China tech, small and mid-caps, semis, consumer discretionary and homebuilders.

Investment professionals’ equity exposure falls to an eight-week low.

NAAIM’s survey* of active managers fell to 72.9 from 78.6, its lowest since mid-September (71.8). It’s now at the 37th percentile of readings since 2016: so managers have trimmed exposure, but they’re a ways from capitulating.

By our calculations, it isn’t an actionable signal at this level. Average S&P 500 returns since 2016 after readings of 70–76, vs. all weeks:

▪ 4 weeks: +1.0% vs. +1.1%.
▪ 13 weeks: +3.7% vs. +3.5%.
▪ 52 weeks: +13.8% vs. +14.1%.
Only readings in the bottom tenth (47 or below) have been followed by notably bigger gains, averaging +20.6% over the next year.

*The index according to NAAIM “represents the average exposure to US Equity markets reported by our members” and ranges from −200% (2x short) to +200% (2x long).

Two more Fed officials signaled on Thursday they see more hikes ahead, but not of the 50 basis point variety. 

New York Fed President and FOMC vice chair John Williams and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly (2027 voter), traditionally in close alignment with the Fed’s old core of Powell, Jefferson and Williams, both spoke Thursday. As a reminder, Williams, an important voice, has been one of the more dovish members, tipping the October hold ahead of time and later noting that he thought a December hike would be the last under his base case.

▪️ Williams on direction: Inflation is “far too high” and stubbornly persistent, and the Fed still has work to do to get policy to the right place (via Bloomberg). That’s a step up from last week’s more subdued “appropriate time to accumulate more information.”

▪️ Williams on pace: The Fed will need to act “over time.” The economy is resilient and getting stronger but not overheating. He didn’t commit to a specific move in December.

▪️ Daly on direction: “My bias is that further tightening will be needed.” “We have a labor market that’s stable, growth that’s good, but we definitely have an inflation problem right now,” with price pressures spreading into services (via Reuters).

▪️ Daly on pace: Rising bond yields “are most welcome,” and tighter financial conditions give the Fed “a little more time to make really calibrated decisions.” On how much and when: “We have many more pieces of data and information over many, many quarters.”

That makes all 10 Fed officials who’ve spoken on the direction of rates since last Thursday’s selloff lean toward more hikes, but they’re split on how fast. I count four camps:

▪️ Quick, and possibly 50bp: Governor Waller, who said a 50bp hike “should be considered” if core CPI is “around 0.3% or even higher,” and that “hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk.”

▪️ Quicker pace, but not pushing for 50bp: Dallas’ Logan, who sees “at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases” and says “it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter,” and Cleveland’s Hammack, who wants “smaller increments, more frequent, smaller rises.”

▪️ Slower pace: New York’s Williams, the FOMC vice chair (act “over time”); San Francisco’s Daly (“a little more time to make really calibrated decisions”); Philadelphia’s Paulson (“further gradual tightening seems appropriate”); Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman (more tightening “has to be carefully weighed against its costs”); and Richmond’s Barkin (“it is wise to move policy with care”).

▪️ Worried about inflation, but don't want to prejudge decisions: Chicago’s Goolsbee (October CPI was “borderline disturbing”) and St. Louis’ Musalem (inflation is “a regressive tax”).

Among the six December voters who’ve weighed in, that’s one for quick and possibly 50bp, two for quicker quarter-point steps and three, including the FOMC vice chair, for a more measured pace. 

That makes 25bp in December the base case, with the real debate over how quickly the next hikes follow which will be teased out in the dot plot. October PCE and November payrolls, both out before the Dec. 8–9 meeting, will be key.

The Day Ahead — PPI and Four Fed Speakers

In US economic data, Friday brings us October PPI.

Fed speakers include Boston Fed President Collins (2028 voter) at 9:10am ET, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman at 10:50am, San Francisco Fed President Daly (2027 voter) at noon and Fed Vice Chair Jefferson at 7pm. Collins and Jefferson are the two we haven’t heard from this week, although Collins is less relevant since she isn’t a voter until 2028.

There are no coupon (>1 year in maturity) Treasury auctions.

No S&P 500 components report.

Ex-US highlights include the second estimate of eurozone third-quarter GDP, final October CPI in France and Spain, Poland’s October CPI and third-quarter GDP, and Brazil’s September retail sales. ECB Executive Board member Schnabel speaks, along with Governing Council members Simkus, Zigman and Sleijpen, and EU leaders hold an informal meeting. Germany’s credit rating is also up for review, and Richemont reports.

BREAKING: The US Treasury posted a -$404 billion budget deficit in October, the largest October deficit in history.

This marks a +$120 billion YoY increase and a +$337 billion surge from October 2024.

This comes as government outlays jumped +$84 billion YoY, to $773 billion, their largest for any October on record.

Defense spending was a major driver, surging +$29 billion YoY, to $129 billion, the largest monthly reading in history.

At the same time, government receipts dropped -$35 billion YoY, to $369 billion.

The US deficit crisis is accelerating.

BREAKING: Retail investors bought +$730 million in Nvidia, $NVDA, stock on Tuesday, their largest daily purchase since March.

This was preceded by +$590 million on Monday and followed by +$300 million on Wednesday.

In total, retail investors bought +$1.6 billion in Nvidia shares in 3 trading days ending Wednesday, retail's largest 3-day purchase in at least 12 months.

Over the same period, the 2x leveraged long Nvidia ETF, $NVDL, attracted +$401 million in inflows, putting it on track for its largest weekly intake since November 2025.

The 2x leveraged long Nvidia ETF, $NVDU, attracted +$64 million, on track for its largest weekly inflow since February 2026.

Meanwhile, during the first 30 minutes of Thursday’s session, retail investors bought +$455 million of $NVDA stock and sold -$345 million, bringing net purchases to +$111 million, their largest in any first 30 minutes of trading on record.

Retail investors are doubling down on Nvidia.

We maintain our view that Jensen Huang and Nvidia prematurely parted ways.

A complete investigation is necessary.

US AI is generating far more revenue than Chinese AI:

As of the end of September, OpenAI and Anthropic had a combined estimated annualized revenue run rate of $105 billion.

This is nearly 10 times the $11 billion generated by 6 Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba, ByteDance, DeepSeek, Z Dot ai, Moonshot AI, and MiniMax.

ByteDance accounted for 36% of this figure at $4 billion.

In Q3 alone, Anthropic's sales grew +47% QoQ, to a record $17 billion.

At the same time, OpenAI revenue surged +50% to a record $10 billion.

By comparison, DeepSeek's annualized revenue run rate doubled in September, but stands at just $1 billion.

US tech firms remain in the lead of the AI race.

Today's PPI is set to show the highest yearly rate since 2022, even if prices are cooling.

Last October's soft reading drops out of the 12-month window, so an expected 0.4% rise lifts the yearly rate from 6.3% to about 6.6%.

The 10-year has already jumped 27bp in four days to 5.10%. And this report captures mid-October, before freight eased and oil fell back below $90.

Watch core against 0.3%. A hot print could push the odds of a half-point Fed hike even higher.
